artiest/hans-rosbaud.text:
Hans Rosbaud was an Austrian conductor, born in Graz on 22 July 1895. He studied at the Hoch Conservatory in Frankfurt, where he learned composition and piano. His first permanent post came in 1921 in Mainz, as musical director of the new music school. In 1928 he became the first principal conductor of the Frankfurt radio orchestra.

Rosbaud is known as a conductor of twentieth-century music. In the 1920s and 1930s he conducted premières of works by Arnold Schönberg and Béla Bartók. Under the Nazi regime he could hardly perform new music any more and kept a low political profile; meanwhile his brother Paul worked as a spy for the Allies. After the war he briefly led the Münchner Philharmoniker and, from 1948 until his death, the radio orchestra in Baden-Baden. In 1954, after only eight days of preparation, he conducted the first performance of Schönberg's opera Moses und Aron, which was released on record in 1957. With his orchestra he travelled to contemporary-music festivals such as Donaueschingen.

He was also a versatile conductor: his recordings include Mahler, Bruckner and Mozart, but also Gluck and Rameau. One magazine called him one of the unsung heroes of mid-twentieth-century music. He died in Lugano on 29 December 1962.
artiest/hans-rosbaud.listen: Listen to Rosbaud's performance of Moses und Aron. Notice how clearly he makes Schönberg's difficult, angular music sound, so that you can keep following the lines in the orchestra.

artiest/hans-zimmer.text: Hans Zimmer (born in Frankfurt in 1957) had no formal musical training. He learned his craft in London, working with synthesizers and as an assistant to the film composer Stanley Myers. With Rain Man (1988) he broke through in Hollywood. For The Lion King (1994) he won an Oscar. He built a studio in Santa Monica, later Remote Control Productions, where he worked with a team of composers. His style blends orchestra, synthesizers and heavy percussion into a single sound. In The Dark Knight (2008) the Joker is a grating note on the cello. For Dune (2021) he used distorted voices and new instruments and won his second Oscar.
artiest/hans-zimmer.listen: Listen to the long build-up: a simple motif or a single note is thickened layer by layer with percussion, synthesizers and orchestra.

artiest/hardfloor.text:
Hardfloor is a German electronic duo made up of Oliver Bondzio and Ramon Zenker. They started in 1991 and broke through a year later with the Hardtrance Acperience EP on the label Harthouse. The track Acperience 1 in particular became a big favourite at raves. The song brought about a brief return of the acid house sound of the 1980s.

That sound revolves around the Roland TB-303, a small bass synthesizer originally intended to imitate a bass guitar. By twisting the filters and accents while playing, you get the squealing, bubbling, squelching sound known as acid. Hardfloor was famous for using up to six of these machines at once. After the debut came albums such as TB Resuscitation (1993) and Home Run (1996), as well as remixes for other artists. In the mid-1990s they also played their acid sound at a slower tempo under the name Da'damn'phreak'noize'phunk. In 1998 they collaborated with Phuture, the Chicago group who had been the first to use the 303 in this way in the 1980s.

Zenker also worked as a producer of commercial dance projects, such as Bellini and Fragma. Hardfloor themselves stayed faithful to hard acid techno. The duo shows how a single instrument can carry an entire genre: a machine that had started out as a failed bass guitar became the lead player in their hands.
artiest/hardfloor.listen: Listen to Acperience 1 and follow the 303 bass line. Notice how the sound slowly changes, from dull to sharp and squealing, while the notes stay almost the same.

artiest/hardwell.text:
Hardwell is the stage name of Robbert van de Corput, a Dutch DJ and producer, born on 7 January 1988 in Breda. The name comes from his father, who translated his surname from Latin and Dutch into English: cor means heart, put means well. For a more appealing sound he changed heart to hard. He had piano lessons at the age of six, and at twelve he made his first tracks in electro while working as a hip hop DJ. He was influenced by Tiësto, who also comes from Breda.

In 2002, at the age of fourteen, he got a record deal with Digidance, the label of the producer duo Klubbheads. His first real single, Play It Around, followed in 2006. In 2009 he made a name for himself with his bootleg of Show Me Love vs. Be. In 2010 he founded the label Revealed Recordings, and in 2011 he started the radio show and podcast Hardwell On Air. DJ Mag named him the best DJ in the world in 2013 and 2014. Spaceman was released in 2012. His debut album United We Are came out in 2015, followed by Rebels Never Die in 2022. In 2018 he announced a break from touring, and in 2022 he returned to the main stage at Ultra Miami.

His music is large-scale electro and big-room house, intended for festival stages. Hardwell belongs to the generation of Dutch DJs who conquered the world after Tiësto, and he showed that dance music could draw a mass audience, with its build-ups, breaks and explosive drop.
artiest/hardwell.listen: Listen to Spaceman and follow the build-up: notice how the track builds tension and then bursts open all at once. How much melody is left when the drop begins?

artiest/hariprasad-chaurasia.text:
Hariprasad Chaurasia is an Indian flautist and composer, born on 1 July 1938 in Allahabad, now Prayagraj. He plays the bansuri, the bamboo flute of the Hindustani classical tradition. His father was a wrestler who wanted him to pursue a career in sport. Chaurasia therefore learned music in secret, first singing with a neighbour and then studying flute for eight years with Bholanath Prasanna in Varanasi.

In 1957 he joined All India Radio in Cuttack, and after four years he was transferred to Bombay. There he worked in both classical music and the Hindi film industry. Later he became a pupil of Annapurna Devi, who made him unlearn what he knew. Chaurasia has played left-handed ever since. He developed the bansuri into a full concert instrument, with techniques that he borrowed from singing and from other instruments.

In 1967 he recorded the album Call of the Valley with the santoor player Shivkumar Sharma and the slide guitarist Brij Bhushan Kabra; it was widely heard in India and beyond. With Sharma he also formed the film-composing duo Shiv-Hari, known for Silsila (1981) and Chandni (1989). He has worked with George Harrison, Zakir Hussain, John McLaughlin and Jan Garbarek, among others, and received high Indian honours, including the Padma Vibhushan in 2000.
artiest/hariprasad-chaurasia.listen: Listen to Call of the Valley. Notice how the bansuri sings like a voice, with long, flowing notes and small ornaments, and how the santoor and the slide guitar play around it.

artiest/haris-alexiou.text:
Haris Alexiou is a Greek singer, born on 27 December 1950. She has lived in Athens since 1958, when her family moved there from Thebes. In the early 1970s she came to prominence in the Greek music world, with a warm, powerful voice and a strong stage presence. A first step was her contribution to the 1972 album Mikra Asia by Apostolos Kaldaras and Pythagoras, alongside George Dalaras.

In 1975, shortly after the fall of the military junta, her first solo album, 12 λαϊκά τραγούδια, was released. It includes Dimitroula, a song from the 1930s that Roza Eskenazi had sung and that has been a standard ever since. That same year she performed in the boîtes of the Plaka, a more intimate way of performing than the big nightclubs. More than thirty albums followed, with titles such as Ξημερώνει, Τα τσίλικα and Εμφύλιος έρωτας, and collaborations with major Greek lyricists and composers.

Alexiou sings laïka, Greek popular song, and also moves through other styles of Greek song. She has performed in theatres on all five continents. She also has an audience in Turkey: songs of hers were sung again there in Turkish. She is regarded as one of the most popular singers in Greece.
artiest/haris-alexiou.listen: Listen to Dimitroula on her album 12 λαϊκά τραγούδια. Notice how she gives an old song from the 1930s new colour with her own voice, and how the accompaniment carries the popular atmosphere.

artiest/harold-arlen.text:
Harold Arlen, born Hyman Arluck, was an American composer of popular music. He was born on 15 February 1905 in Buffalo, New York, the son of a Jewish cantor, and died on 23 April 1986. He learned to play the piano, formed a small band at fifteen and left home as a teenager. In the early 1920s he moved to New York, worked as an accompanist in vaudeville and took the name Harold Arlen.

His first well-known song was Get Happy from 1929, with lyrics by Ted Koehler. With Koehler he wrote shows for the Cotton Club in Harlem, and from that partnership came standards such as Let's Fall in Love and Stormy Weather. In the mid-1930s he worked increasingly in Hollywood, where he found E. Y. Harburg as a lyricist. Together they wrote the songs for the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz, including Over the Rainbow, for which they won an Oscar for best original song. He also wrote Happiness Is a Thing Called Joe for the film Cabin in the Sky.

Arlen wrote more than five hundred songs and is counted among the Great American Songbook. His melodies lean on blues and jazz, which links the American theatre song with the Black music of his day. Over the Rainbow was named the song of the twentieth century by the RIAA and the NEA.
artiest/harold-arlen.listen: Listen to Over the Rainbow in the film version of The Wizard of Oz. Notice the big leap in the opening melody, and how that leap makes the longing in the lyrics audible.

artiest/harold-faltermeyer.text: Harold Faltermeyer, from Munich, studied at the music conservatoire there and worked as a keyboard player and arranger for Giorgio Moroder, on films including Midnight Express and American Gigolo. His own breakthrough was Beverly Hills Cop (1984). The instrumental theme Axel F, with a bouncy synthesizer melody and a tight drum-machine rhythm, became a worldwide hit. The album won a Grammy. He then wrote the music for the comedy Fletch (1985) and for Top Gun (1986). The Top Gun Anthem, with guitarist Steve Stevens, won a Grammy in 1987. Faltermeyer turned synthesizer pop into the standard sound of the Hollywood action film.
artiest/harold-faltermeyer.listen: Notice the short, rhythmic synthesizer melody over a tightly programmed drum-machine rhythm.

artiest/harold-land.text:
Harold Land was an American tenor saxophonist in hard bop and post-bop. He was born on 18 December 1928 in Houston, Texas, grew up in San Diego and began playing at sixteen. He started out on the R&B circuit and in 1949 made his first recordings as a leader, the Harold Land All-Stars for Savoy Records.

In 1954 he joined the quintet of Max Roach and Clifford Brown, a band at the forefront of the development of hard bop. Land also wrote his own compositions for it. In 1955 he moved to Los Angeles, where he played with Curtis Counce and led his own groups, sometimes together with Bobby Hutcherson, Blue Mitchell or Red Mitchell. Albums from this period include Harold in the Land of Jazz from 1958 and The Fox from 1960. From the 1970s on, the influence of John Coltrane became increasingly audible in his playing. In the 1980s he played regularly with the Timeless All Stars.

Land had a dark, strong tone that also revealed something fragile. His sound started somewhere between rhythm and blues and Coleman Hawkins, and later absorbed Coltrane's harmonies and modal thinking. From 1996 he taught in the Jazz Studies programme at UCLA. He died on 27 July 2001.
artiest/harold-land.listen: Listen to The Fox. Notice the dark, almost sombre tone of the tenor saxophone and how Land uses it to build a solo of his own, full of restraint.

artiest/harold-melvin-en-the-blue-notes.text:
Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes was an American soul group from Philadelphia. The group began in the mid-1950s as The Charlemagnes and took the name The Blue Notes in 1954, with Harold Melvin as its founder. For years the ensemble recorded for all kinds of labels without a breakthrough. It changed line-up often and had only minor successes in the 1960s.

The turning point came in 1970, when Teddy Pendergrass joined the band as drummer and soon became lead singer. In 1972 the group signed to Philadelphia International, the label of the writers and producers Gamble and Huff. There came success with If You Don't Know Me by Now (1972), a ballad that sold more than a million copies. The Love I Lost (1973), Bad Luck and Wake Up Everybody (both 1975) followed. The last two show the other side of the group: danceable soul with a social message. Bad Luck stayed at the top of the Hot Dance Music/Club Play chart for eleven weeks, a record. All four albums on Philadelphia International went gold.

In 1976 Pendergrass left after a row over money and began a solo career. Melvin carried on with new singers until his death in 1997. The group is regarded as one of the most popular representatives of 1970s Philadelphia soul, with layered backing vocals, rich strings and warm lead vocals as its trademarks. With his solo work, Pendergrass himself became a major name in soul.
artiest/harold-melvin-en-the-blue-notes.listen: Listen to If You Don't Know Me by Now and notice how Teddy Pendergrass's lead vocal builds from restrained to almost pleading, while the backing vocals and strings give him more and more room.

artiest/harold-shapero.text:
Harold Shapero was an American composer, born on 29 April 1920 in Lynn, Massachusetts. He played the piano as a child and for a time was a pianist in dance orchestras. With a friend he founded the Hal Kenny Orchestra, a swing-era jazz band. His heart, however, lay with classical music. He was taught by Nicolas Slonimsky and Ernst Krenek, among others, went to Harvard at eighteen and studied with Walter Piston. Later he worked with Paul Hindemith and Nadia Boulanger. At Harvard he became friends with Leonard Bernstein.

His Nine-Minute Overture was performed at Tanglewood in 1940, conducted by Aaron Copland, and won him the Rome Prize in 1941. In the 1940s he wrote a great deal, including three piano sonatas, a violin sonata and chamber music. His major work was the Symphony for Classical Orchestra, a symphony of about forty-five minutes in four movements. Bernstein conducted the première in January 1948 with the Boston Symphony Orchestra and recorded the work in 1953. After that it was largely forgotten, until André Previn brought it back in 1986.

Shapero belongs to the American composers who used classical forms with a contemporary, American voice. He died on 17 May 2013. His experience of swing jazz and of rigorous classical technique makes him an example of border-crossing between worlds.
artiest/harold-shapero.listen: Listen to Symphony for Classical Orchestra. Notice how clear and classical the form is, and try to hear where you nevertheless recognise something American in the rhythm and the melody.

artiest/harrie-jekkers.text:
Harrie Jekkers was born on 1 July 1951 in the Schilderswijk district of The Hague and grew up in Moerwijk. He studied English in Groningen and then spent a few years teaching in Utrecht. When that did not suit him very well, he began writing songs and lyrics, encouraged by his father.

In 1978, with Koos Meinderts, he founded 't Klein Orkest after the group Groot Orkest had fallen apart. The group came out of the world of cabaret and sang in Dutch about ordinary people and big questions. The breakthrough came with Over de muur, a song about divided Berlin that Jekkers had wanted to write as neutrally as possible, but which nevertheless became known as a protest song. In 1982, under the pseudonym Harry Klorkestein, an anagram of Klein Orkest, he had a big hit with O, o, Den Haag. That song is still regarded as the unofficial anthem of The Hague. The album Later is allang begonnen was released in 1984.

In 1985 't Klein Orkest broke up and Jekkers became a cabaret performer, again with lyrics he wrote together with Meinderts. He also wrote for Kinderen voor Kinderen and for children's theatre. Later he appeared in theatres with Jeroen van Merwijk, and from 2017 to 2019 Klein Orkest went on a comeback tour. Jekkers combines the humour and precision of cabaret with the simplicity of the pop song. Since 2001 he has lived in Ibiza.
artiest/harrie-jekkers.listen: Listen to Over de muur by Klein Orkest. Notice how Jekkers, without grand words, describes what people on either side of the wall see and miss, and the calm, almost narrative pace of the song.

artiest/harry-belafonte.text:
Harry Belafonte was born in Harlem, New York, in 1927 as Harold George Bellanfanti. His parents came from Jamaica, and from 1932 to 1940 he lived with his grandmother on that island. Back in New York he left secondary school and served in the Navy in the Second World War. Afterwards he fell under the spell of the theatre. He took acting lessons, alongside Sidney Poitier and Marlon Brando among others, and in 1954 received a Tony Award for his role in a Broadway revue.

As a singer, Belafonte made Caribbean calypso popular with a worldwide audience. His album Calypso (1956) was the first LP by a single artist to sell more than a million copies. It includes Day-O (The Banana Boat Song) and Jamaica Farewell. Later came Mary's Boy Child and Jump in the Line (Shake, Senora), among others. He also sang blues, folk, gospel and American standards, and acted in films such as Carmen Jones (1954) and Island in the Sun (1957).

Belafonte was not only an artist but also an activist. He saw the singer and actor Paul Robeson as his example and in the 1950s and 1960s was a confidant of Martin Luther King in the civil rights movement. In this way he linked his fame to political ideals, far beyond America as well. He died in 2023. A year earlier he had been inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, as one of the artists who influenced early popular music.
artiest/harry-belafonte.listen: Listen to Jump in the Line (Shake, Senora) and notice the skipping calypso rhythm and the horns. Hear how Belafonte and the chorus answer each other, like a question and an answer.

artiest/harry-carney.text:
Harry Carney was a jazz saxophonist and clarinettist who played for more than forty years in Duke Ellington's orchestra. He was born on 1 April 1910 in Boston and grew up close to Johnny Hodges, his later colleague. He started on piano at seven, switched to clarinet at fourteen and took up the alto saxophone a year later. His models included Buster Bailey, Sidney Bechet and Don Murray.

At seventeen he played with Ellington for the first time, in Boston in 1927, and in October of that year made his first recordings with him. He stayed with the band until the end of his life. From 1928 the baritone saxophone became his main instrument, and on that instrument he was for a long time without real rivals, until the bebop era in the mid-1940s. He co-wrote Rockin' in Rhythm and played the bubbling clarinet solo in it. Later he also took up the bass clarinet.

In the sound of the Ellington orchestra, Carney's baritone often filled in voices above the obvious low register, which changed the colour of the whole. Ellington wrote many pieces for him, and in 1973 he built the Third Sacred Concert around his instrument. Carney was also the man who drove Ellington across the country. He died on 8 October 1974, four months after Ellington.
artiest/harry-carney.listen: Listen to Rockin' in Rhythm by the Ellington orchestra. Notice the clarinet solo that Carney co-wrote, and then try to hear the deep, round sound of his baritone saxophone in other pieces by the band.

artiest/harry-gregson-williams.text: Harry Gregson-Williams was born in Chichester in 1961. At the age of seven he won a music scholarship to St John's College School in Cambridge, where he was a chorister. Later he went to Stowe School on a music scholarship and studied at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London. He is the older brother of the composer Rupert Gregson-Williams. He wrote music for the animated films Antz (1998), Chicken Run (2000) and Shrek (2001). For Shrek he won an Annie Award together with John Powell. He often worked with the directors Ridley and Tony Scott, for example on Kingdom of Heaven (2005) and The Martian (2015). He also wrote the music for two Narnia films and for the game series Metal Gear Solid.
artiest/harry-gregson-williams.listen: Notice how he blends orchestra, choir and electronic pulses, and how in Kingdom of Heaven he adds the viol consort Fretwork and the voice of Natacha Atlas.

artiest/harry-miller.text:
Harry Miller was a South African jazz double bassist who lived in England for most of his adult life. He was born on 25 April 1941 in Cape Town. His career began as the bassist of the rock group Manfred Mann. After moving to London he became part of a circle of musicians who in the 1960s and 1970s combined free jazz with the music of South Africa.

He recorded with Elton Dean, Chris McGregor, Louis Moholo, John Surman, Keith Tippett and Mike Westbrook, among others, and also led a group of his own, Isipingo, named after a holiday resort in South Africa. In 1971 he appeared as a guest on Islands by the progressive rock band King Crimson. His own albums from those years include Children at Play from 1974 and Bracknell Breakdown from 1978. Together with his wife he founded the label Ogun Records, an important platform for this British and South African jazz.

At the end of the 1970s Miller moved to the Netherlands for financial reasons, where he played with musicians from Willem Breuker's circle. He was killed in a car accident in the Netherlands on 16 December 1983.
artiest/harry-miller.listen: Listen to Children at Play. Notice the double bass: how Miller lets the rhythms of South African music move along in a free-jazz setting.

artiest/harry-muskee.text:
Harry Muskee was born in Assen in 1941, in the middle of the war. His father had been taken to Germany as a prisoner of war, and Harry did not see him until he was four. His mother had multiple sclerosis, and his father, a fire chief, was often away from home. As a result he was cared for mainly by his grandmother. He had guitar lessons at fifteen, and at school he fell under the spell of jazz and Dixieland. With the brothers Henk and Jaap Hilbrandie he played at school parties in Assen.

Via the station American Forces Network, meant for American soldiers in Germany, Muskee first heard the blues. When he found a record by John Lee Hooker, recorded live at the Newport festival, he knew that he wanted to make this music. With guitarist Eelco Gelling he founded Cuby + Blizzards. The debut album Desolation won an Edison, and Appleknockers Flophouse (1969) is regarded as a high point of Dutch blues. After the group broke up in 1972 he played in Red White 'n Blue and the Muskee Gang, among others, and later toured for years again as Cuby + Blizzards, with guitarist Erwin Java.

Muskee sang the blues in English, but from the Drenthe countryside. He stayed true to the music and made a journey through the American South for Radio Drenthe, in search of the roots of the blues. A bust of him stands in Grolloo. He died in 2011.
artiest/harry-muskee.listen: Listen to a track from Appleknockers Flophouse by Cuby + Blizzards and notice Harry Muskee's voice. Hear how he sings American blues, with Eelco Gelling's raw guitar alongside.

artiest/harry-styles.text:
Harry Styles is an English singer, songwriter and actor, born in Redditch in 1994 and raised in the village of Holmes Chapel in Cheshire. As a child he sang along to his grandfather's karaoke machine, and the first song he recorded was The Girl of My Best Friend by Elvis Presley. In 2010 he auditioned for The X Factor as a solo artist. He was eliminated, but was put into a group with four other rejected boys. Styles came up with the name: One Direction. The boy band became one of the most successful in the world and went on hiatus in 2016.

Styles then began a solo career. His debut Harry Styles (2017) opened with Sign of the Times, a power ballad with glam rock influences that was compared to David Bowie. The album leaned on the soft rock of the 1970s. On Fine Line (2019) funk and soul were added, with Watermelon Sugar as his first number 1 in the United States. Harry's House (2022) won the Grammy for album of the year, and the single As It Was became the biggest hit of that year worldwide. In 2026 came Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.

Styles shows how a pop star from a television programme can grow into an artist with a face of his own. His music often looks back to the rock and pop of the 1970s, but sounds contemporary thanks to modern production. He also stands out for his flamboyant clothing, with which he probed the boundaries between menswear and womenswear. He has also acted in films such as Dunkirk (2017).
artiest/harry-styles.listen: Listen to As It Was (2022) and compare it with a rock 'n' roll song by Elvis Presley. Notice the sound of the instruments, the tempo and how the production surrounds the voice.

artiest/harry-warren.text: Harry Warren (1893–1981) was born Salvatore Guaragna in Brooklyn and taught himself music. In the 1930s he wrote, with the lyricist Al Dubin, the songs for the Warner Bros. musicals for which Busby Berkeley created the big dance numbers. In 42nd Street (1933) and Gold Diggers of 1933 you hear optimistic songs such as We're in the Money, in the middle of the economic crisis. Later he wrote Chattanooga Choo Choo for 20th Century Fox, played by Glenn Miller in Sun Valley Serenade (1941). For MGM came The Harvey Girls (1946). He won three Oscars for best song, but his name remained less well known than his melodies.
artiest/harry-warren.listen: Notice the tight song form with a catchy chorus and how the swinging accompaniment imitates the movement of a train or a dance troupe.

artiest/harvey-brooks.text:
Harvey Oliver Brooks was an American pianist and composer, born on 17 February 1899 and died on 17 June 1968. He toured and recorded in the early 1920s with the singer Mamie Smith and then settled in California. From 1923 he led the Quality Four together with Paul Howard, a quartet with a female singer, named after the Quality Cafe in Los Angeles. He stayed with that group and with Howard's Quality Serenaders, with whom he also made recordings, until 1930.

From 1931 to 1935 Brooks was musical director of Les Hite's orchestra. In that role he worked for Hollywood studios and wrote film music. He was the first Black American to write the complete score for a major feature film: I'm No Angel from 1933, starring Mae West. Later he led a band of his own, played with Kid Ory from 1952 and recorded with Teddy Buckner and Joe Darensbourg.

From 1961 he was a member of the Young Men of New Orleans, a Dixieland group, which he led during the last year of his life. His place in history is that of a pioneer in Hollywood: a Black musician who, in a closed world, opened the way for later film composers. In the Netflix series Big Mouth he appears as the man who accompanies the young Duke Ellington.
artiest/harvey-brooks.listen: Listen to Stuff by Paul Howard's Quality Serenaders from 1929, with music by Brooks. Notice the stomping rhythm and how the band works with short solos and a vocal part by Lionel Hampton.

artiest/harvey-mason.text:
Harvey Mason is an American jazz drummer and producer, born on 22 February 1947 in Atlantic City, New Jersey. He started on drums at a young age, with the support of his father, who was a drummer in an army band. He studied for a time at Berklee and then at the New England Conservatory, where Vic Firth was one of his teachers. Later he received an honorary doctorate from Berklee.

Mason was the first drummer of The Headhunters, the fusion band around Herbie Hancock, and played on the album Head Hunters. He then became a much-in-demand studio musician. He played on records by Bill Withers, George Benson, Lee Ritenour, Barbra Streisand, Frank Sinatra and Notorious B.I.G., among others, and produced the group Seawind. Together with Bob James, Lee Ritenour and bassist Nathan East he founded the jazz group Fourplay, and albums released under his own name include Marching in the Street from 1975, Funk in a Mason Jar from 1977 and Chameleon from 2014.

Mason's playing combines the swing of jazz with the tight groove of funk and soul. He names Art Blakey, Max Roach, Tony Williams and Steve Gadd as his models. His significance lies in the foundation: on many recordings where you would not immediately guess it, his drum pattern lies beneath the whole.
artiest/harvey-mason.listen: Listen to Chameleon by Herbie Hancock on Head Hunters. Notice the drum pattern beneath the bass riff: how steady the rhythm stays while the synthesizers above play freely.

artiest/haydn-quartet.text:
The Haydn Quartet was an American vocal quartet from the early days of sound recording. Around 1900 the group recorded for the Victor label and was among the first singers to reach a large audience through recordings, even before radio existed. The name refers to the composer Joseph Haydn and was meant to give the group a dignified ring. Please note: this is therefore something different from the Haydn Quartets by Mozart, which are not what this encyclopedia means.

The singers performed the popular songs of their time in four-part harmony, without instrumental accompaniment or with a simple accompaniment. The repertoire consisted of sentimental ballads, hymns and light numbers. Sweet Adeline, recorded in 1904, became their best-known record. The song grew into a firm favourite of barbershop quartets and is still sung in that tradition to this day.

For pop history this group matters mainly as an example of the first recording industry. Vocal quartets were among the most popular kinds of recording in those years, because singing stood up well to the limited technology of the wax cylinder and the gramophone. The tight ensemble singing, in which the voices complement one another almost like instruments, returns later in doo-wop, gospel and soul.
artiest/haydn-quartet.listen: Listen to Sweet Adeline and notice how the four voices together form a single chord. Try to hear which voice carries the melody and which voices fill in around it.

artiest/head-hunters.text:
Head Hunters is the album that pianist Herbie Hancock released on Columbia in 1973, and also the name of the band that plays on it. Hancock had just made three experimental records with his Mwandishi sextet and wanted to play something lighter, more down to earth. In San Francisco he put together a new group: reed player Bennie Maupin, bassist Paul Jackson, drummer Harvey Mason and percussionist Bill Summers. That group became known as the Headhunters.

The album has only four pieces. Chameleon revolves around a bass line that Hancock plays on an ARP Odyssey synthesizer. Watermelon Man is a new version of his 1962 hit, with African percussion and Summers blowing across a beer bottle. Sly is dedicated to Sly Stone, and Vein Melter is a slow piece with Fender Rhodes and bass clarinet. There is no guitar: the Hohner Clavinet takes over that role. Jackson and Mason lay a tight, relaxed funk groove beneath it.

Head Hunters brought jazz-funk and fusion to a large audience and was for a long time the best-selling jazz album. Purists considered it a betrayal, but the record became a model for funk, soul and later hip hop. The band continued to work with Hancock on albums such as Thrust (1974) and also made records of their own, such as Survival of the Fittest (1975). In 2008 the album was added to the archive of the American Library of Congress.
artiest/head-hunters.listen: Listen to Chameleon on Head Hunters (1973). Notice the bass line: it does not come from a bass guitar but from a synthesizer, and around it clavinet, drums and horns build up a funk groove layer by layer.

artiest/headhunterz.text:
Headhunterz is the alias of Willem Rebergen, a Dutch DJ and producer, born on 12 September 1985 in Veenendaal. He became hooked on hardstyle in 2003 when he went to Qlimax with friends. With his friend Bobby van Putten he formed the duo Nasty D-Tuners, which won a Defqon.1 DJ competition in 2004. At the end of 2005 they signed to Scantraxx, and the first record under the name Headhunterz was released in 2006. Rebergen then continued solo and was given the sub-label Scantraxx Reloaded.

In 2007 he made his first big anthem for Qlimax, The Power of the Mind. In 2008, with Wildstylez, came the album Project One, which helped determine the direction of hardstyle in the following years, with trance-like synthesizer melodies and heavily processed, pitched kicks. In 2013 he started the label HARD with STYLE and signed to the American Ultra Music. His own albums are Sacrifice from 2012 and The Return of Headhunterz from 2018. In 2017 he returned to the hardstyle scene, and in 2018 he and Wildstylez started the label Art of Creation.

Headhunterz has performed at festivals such as Defqon.1, Qlimax, Hard Bass, Electric Daisy Carnival and Tomorrowland. He is one of the faces who turned hardstyle from a Dutch club sound into an international festival genre. He also works as a voice actor.
artiest/headhunterz.listen: Listen to The Power of the Mind. Notice the heavy, distorted kick and how the melody in the chorus rises above the rhythm.

artiest/headhunterz-en-wildstylez.text:
Headhunterz and Wildstylez are two Dutch hardstyle producers who in 2008 started the project Project One together. Wildstylez's real name is Joram Metekohy, born in 1983. He first made hardstyle under the name Seizure and released his first solo record at the end of 2007 on Scantraxx Reloaded, Headhunterz's sub-label. That is where the two producers met.

Their first joint release, Blame It on the Music / Project 1, came out in early 2008 and was a hit. That gave them the incentive to make an entire album. In less than three months, roughly one track a week, they made the album Headhunterz & Wildstylez Present: Project One. It was released on 25 July 2008 on CD and digitally. Tracks such as Life Beyond Earth and The Art of Creation became dance-floor classics in the hardstyle scene. A tour and several compilations followed.

In 2009 came Tonight, the collaboration with Noisecontrollers, which later finished high in the Q-dance polls for the best hardstyle tracks. Wildstylez later founded labels of his own, including Lose Control Music, and in 2018 he started the label Art of Creation with Headhunterz.

Hardstyle combines a hard, distorted kick drum with a melodic, often euphoric lead. The duo belongs to the generation that established this Dutch genre at large festivals such as Defqon.1.
artiest/headhunterz-en-wildstylez.listen: Listen to Blame It on the Muzic and follow the kick drum: hear how it sets the beat like a hard, distorted thump, while the melody above keeps building towards the drop.

artiest/hector-berlioz.text:
Hector Berlioz was a French composer, conductor and critic of the Romantic era. He was born on 11 December 1803 as the eldest son of a physician. He was meant to become a doctor himself and studied medicine in Paris, but chose music against his family's wishes. His independence of mind brought him into conflict with the conservative musical world of Paris. In 1830 he nevertheless won the Prix de Rome.

At twenty-four he fell in love with the Irish Shakespearean actress Harriet Smithson, whom he pursued for seven years until she accepted him. She inspired the Symphonie fantastique, his first great success, in which an idealised image of her keeps returning as an idée fixe. He also wrote Harold en Italie, a Requiem, Roméo et Juliette, La Damnation de Faust and the operas Benvenuto Cellini, Les Troyens and Béatrice et Bénédict, among others. Les Troyens was so large that it was never performed in full in his lifetime. Because he had only occasional success in France, he increasingly became a conductor, with an international reputation. His Treatise on Instrumentation of 1844 later influenced many composers.

Berlioz died in Paris in 1869. He wrote programmatic music for a large orchestra with new colours, and that makes him a forerunner of later film music and of the idea that an orchestra can tell a story.
artiest/hector-berlioz.listen: Listen to the Symphonie fantastique. Notice the idée fixe, the melody that you keep hearing again in different forms, and how the orchestra colours it differently each time.

artiest/hector-lavoe.text:
Héctor Lavoe, born Héctor Juan Pérez Martínez, was a Puerto Rican salsa singer. He was born in 1946 in Ponce, Puerto Rico, into a musical family, and had lessons at a music school there. In 1963, at the age of sixteen, he moved to New York. There he sang in various groups, including with Johnny Pacheco, before his big chance came.

In 1967 he became the singer in Willie Colón's band. Together they made hits such as El Malo and Canto a Borinquen. Later Lavoe went solo and formed an orchestra of his own. As a soloist he recorded El cantante, written by Rubén Blades, Bandolera by Colón and Periódico de ayer by Tite Curet Alonso, among others. He also frequently appeared as a guest singer with the Fania All-Stars, the star ensemble of the Fania label. His solo work ran from Cosa nuestra (1969) and La voz (1975) to Comedia (1978), the album on which El cantante appears.

Lavoe was known for his clear, sharp voice, his good diction and his sense of improvisation over the rhythms of the band, with brass, percussion and piano as the main sound. His life was marked by addiction and illness, and he died in 1993. Many experts count him among the most important and influential singers of salsa, and a large part of the genre owes its fame in the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s partly to his voice.
artiest/hector-lavoe.listen: Listen to El cantante and notice how Lavoe tells the singer's story: how his voice moves freely above the tight percussion and brass.

artiest/heino.text:
Heino, whose real name is Heinz Georg Kramm, is a German singer of Schlager and traditional Volksmusik. He was born in Düsseldorf in 1938. His father was killed in the Second World War and his mother gave him an accordion when he was ten. He first became a baker and pastry chef, and in 1961 he sang in the trio OK Singers. His stage name comes from his sister Hannelore, who as a child could not pronounce his first names Heinz Georg properly.

In the mid-1960s Heino broke through and since then he has appeared in the German charts many times. He often performed on German TV programmes such as the ZDF-Hitparade and Musikantenstadl. Most of his repertoire consists of pop versions of old folk songs. Blau blüht der Enzian from 1972 is the best-known example: an arrangement of the folk song Das Schweizermadel. Albums such as Kein schöner Land in dieser Zeit (1967) and Die schönsten Volkslieder der Welt (1972) showcase this repertoire.

His trademarks are a low baritone voice, blond hair and dark sunglasses, which he wears because of an eye condition. In 2013 he surprised everyone with Mit freundlichen Grüßen, an album of covers of artists including Die Ärzte, Peter Fox and Rammstein, which for the first time reached number 1 in Germany. In 2018, after fifty years, he announced a farewell tour. Heino shows how the German folk song could live on in popular culture.
artiest/heino.listen: Listen to Blau blüht der Enzian and notice the heavy baritone voice and the simple, singable melody. Can you hear that it is a folk song dressed up in a pop jacket?

artiest/heinrich-scheidemann.text:
Heinrich Scheidemann was a German organist and composer, born around 1595 in Wöhrden in Holstein. His father was an organist in Wöhrden and Hamburg. From 1611 to 1614 he studied in Amsterdam with Sweelinck, and he was apparently one of his favourite pupils, for Sweelinck dedicated a canon to him. By 1629 at the latest he was organist of the Catharinenkirche in Hamburg, a post he held for more than thirty years, until his death in 1663 during an outbreak of plague.

Scheidemann was the best-known organ composer in northern Germany in his day. Unlike many German contemporaries, such as Praetorius, Schütz, Scheidt and Schein, he wrote almost exclusively for the organ. Of no composer of his time has so much organ music survived. His lasting contribution is his settings of Lutheran chorales, in three types: chorale settings with a cantus firmus, an early form of the chorale prelude; settings in the style of monody; and extended chorale fantasias, a new form that made use of the growing German Baroque organ. He also wrote Magnificat settings for alternating performance with the choir during vespers.

His pupils included Johann Adam Reincken, who succeeded him in Hamburg, and possibly Dieterich Buxtehude. Scheidemann is thus regarded as an important forerunner of Buxtehude and Johann Sebastian Bach.
artiest/heinrich-scheidemann.listen: Listen to Christ lag in Todesbanden on the organ. Notice how the familiar chorale melody keeps returning, surrounded by the other voices of the organ.

artiest/heinrich-schutz.text:
Heinrich Schütz was a German composer of the early Baroque, born in 1585 and died in 1672. He was regarded as the most important German composer of the seventeenth century before Johann Sebastian Bach. He studied in Venice with Giovanni Gabrieli and brought the Italian style to Germany. His first Italian madrigals appeared in 1611. For most of his life he worked as Kapellmeister at the court of the Elector of Saxony in Dresden.

His work is almost entirely vocal and religious. Well known are the Psalmen Davids for several choirs and instruments from 1619, the Kleine geistliche Konzerte and the Deutsches Magnificat. Schütz sought a way to sing the German text of Luther and the Bible expressively, with the dramatic force of the Italian madrigal.

Schütz is regarded as the composer who brought the Italian Baroque to Germany and gave it a German form of its own. His music paved the way for the great organists and cantor-composers who came after him, up to and including Johann Sebastian Bach.
artiest/heinrich-schutz.listen: Listen to a movement from the Psalmen Davids. Notice how the two choirs toss the phrases to each other, a technique Schütz learned in Venice.

artiest/heitor-villa-lobos.text: As a young man, Heitor Villa-Lobos played cello and guitar in orchestras in Rio and spent time with the chorões, the street musicians of choro. He worked that music into his classical output: in the 1920s he wrote a series of Chôros. In the Bachianas Brasileiras he joined Bach with Brazilian melodies. The fifth, for soprano and eight cellos, became his best-known work.
artiest/heitor-villa-lobos.listen: Listen to the Aria from Bachianas Brasileiras No. 5: eight cellos pluck like guitars, and the soprano sings a long, wordless melody above them.

artiest/helen-reddy.text:
Helen Reddy was an Australian-American singer, actress, presenter and activist, born on 25 October 1941 in Melbourne into a theatrical family. Her mother was an actress, singer and dancer, her father a writer, producer and actor. She was on stage at the age of four. In 1966 she won a talent contest on the programme Bandstand, the prize being a trip to New York and an audition. The audition came to nothing. She ended up, via Chicago, in Los Angeles, where her first singles appeared in 1968 and 1970. The B-side of the second, I Don't Know How to Love Him, did well, and a year later she signed with Capitol Records.

In the 1970s she had international success, especially in the United States: fifteen singles reached the top forty of the Billboard Hot 100, and three went to number one. Her best-known song is I Am Woman, from 1972, which became an anthem of second-wave feminism. She became a feminist figurehead. In 1974, at the first American Music Awards, she won the award for favourite female pop and rock artist. On television she became the first Australian to host a weekly hour-long prime-time show on an American network.

In the 1980s and 1990s she appeared in musicals. In 2002 she stopped performing. She studied, worked as a hypnotherapist and returned to the stage in 2011. Reddy died on 29 September 2020.
artiest/helen-reddy.listen: Listen to I Am Woman. Notice how calmly and confidently she sings the chorus, and what that tone does to the lyrics.

artiest/helmut-franz.text:
Helmut Franz was a German conductor and teacher, best known as a choral conductor. He was born in 1911 and died on 30 January 2002. He worked as Kapellmeister at the Hessisches Landestheater in Darmstadt and taught there at the Akademie für Tonkunst. In 1966 he became head of the NDR Chor in Hamburg, the choir of the broadcaster Norddeutscher Rundfunk. He succeeded Max Thurn and remained until 1987.

Franz focused the choir on a cappella music and on contemporary music. He began the concert series das neue werk. In 1967 he conducted Lux aeterna by György Ligeti, a piece for sixteen-part unaccompanied choir. That recording became known as music in Stanley Kubrick's film 2001: A Space Odyssey and was released in 1968 in the Avantgarde collection of Deutsche Grammophon. Under his direction came premières of Penderecki's Utrenja and of Hans Werner Henze's Das Floß der Medusa, in 1968, a performance that was interrupted by political protest in the hall.

Franz saw a broadcasting choir as a group of specialists who sing modern works that other choirs cannot manage for lack of time or ability. In the 1970s the choir was a guest at festivals, including with Stockhausen's Atmen gibt das Leben. He was also a professor of opera in Hamburg.
artiest/helmut-franz.listen: Listen to Lux aeterna by Ligeti. Notice how the voices slide into one another very slowly and you can hardly make out individual notes any more, only a glowing sound.

artiest/helmut-walcha.text:
Helmut Walcha was a blind German organist, harpsichordist, teacher and composer, specialising in the Dutch and German Baroque. He was born on 27 October 1907 in Leipzig. After a smallpox vaccination his sight slowly deteriorated, and at nineteen he was completely blind. Even so, he studied at the Leipzig conservatoire and became an assistant to Günther Ramin at the Thomaskirche, Bach's church.

In 1929 he took a post in Frankfurt am Main, at the Friedenskirche, and he stayed there for the rest of his life. From 1938 he was professor of organ at the Musikhochschule and from 1946 organist of the Dreikönigskirche. He recorded the complete keyboard works of Johann Sebastian Bach twice, first in mono between 1947 and 1952 and then in stereo from 1956 to 1971, all from memory. His own ending for the last fugue of Die Kunst der Fuge was later also recorded by his pupil George Ritchie. Walcha himself wrote four volumes of chorale preludes and arrangements of orchestral works.

He taught many American organists who came to Germany, including several Fulbright students. In 1981 he stopped performing and in 1991 he died in Frankfurt. His Bach recordings are still regarded as a benchmark.
artiest/helmut-walcha.listen: Listen to the Toccata und Fuge d-moll BWV 565 on Helmut Walcha spielt Bach. Notice how clearly he lets the voices in the fugue sound, even though he plays everything from memory.

artiest/hemant-kumar.text:
Hemant Kumar, known in Bengali as Hemanta Mukherjee, was an Indian music director and playback singer. He was born on 16 June 1920 in Varanasi, grew up in Calcutta and died on 26 September 1989. He left an engineering course to choose music. His debut as a playback singer came in 1940 with the Bengali film Rajkumarer Nirbbasan under S.D. Burman. He sang mainly in Bengali and Hindi, but also in many other Indian languages.

In 1944 he recorded his first album of songs by Rabindranath Tagore, and he became one of the most important interpreters of Rabindra Sangeet. In 1947 he had a turning point with Gayer Badhu, a six-minute song by Salil Chowdhury about the consequences of the Bengal famine, which filled both sides of a record. In 1951 he moved to Bombay. There he composed for, among others, Nagin in 1954, a film that was a great success mainly because of its music and won him a Filmfare Award for best music director in 1955. As a singer he often worked with S.D. Burman and sang for actors such as Dev Anand, Sunil Dutt and Biswajeet. In Bengal he formed a much-loved duo with the actor Uttam Kumar.

He won two national awards for best male playback singer. His deep, warm voice earned him the nickname Voice of God.
artiest/hemant-kumar.listen: Listen to Rabindra Sangeet in his performance or to songs from Nagin. Notice his deep, warm voice and how calmly he lets each line fade out.

artiest/henk-temming.text:
Henk Temming is a Dutch singer, composer, lyricist and producer, born in 1951 in Utrecht. He grew up in the Dichterswijk district of Utrecht; his father, who was also called Henk Temming, was a professional footballer at DOS. Temming started in a hobby band with Sander van Herk, in which it soon became mostly his own songs that were played. After that band the two started Het Goede Doel, and shortly afterwards Henk Westbroek joined.

With Het Goede Doel, Temming had a series of hits in Dutch in the 1980s, such as België and Vriendschap. He also produced the group's albums, from Tempo Doeloe (1983) to Souvenir (1989). In 1982 the two singers made the single Sinterklaas, wie kent hem niet as Henk en Henk. In 1987 Temming started the StuStuStudio in Utrecht with Van Herk. There he produced work for Linda de Mol, Paul de Leeuw, De Kast, Herman van Veen and Kinderen voor Kinderen, among others. For Linda de Mol he wrote Beethoven, for De Kast Woorden zonder woorden, among others. In 1991 he made the programme De Hulpsinterklaas for the broadcaster TROS, of which an album was also released.

Temming is above all a man behind the controls: someone who writes songs and lets others sound good. In doing so he left a considerable mark on Dutch-language pop of the 1980s and 1990s. Later he produced the music for De Vrienden van Amstel LIVE! and sat on the jury of the first season of X Factor. Since 2008 he has performed again with Westbroek as Het Goede Doel.
artiest/henk-temming.listen: Listen to België by Het Goede Doel. Notice how synthesizers and drums form the foundation and how the Dutch lyrics lie over it like a pop melody.

artiest/henk-westbroek.text:
Henk Westbroek is a Dutch singer, lyricist, radio presenter and entrepreneur, born in 1952 in Zuilen, which is now part of Utrecht. He grew up in a poor family and studied sociology in Utrecht. While still a student he performed in left-wing circles. In the late 1970s he formed the band Het Goede Doel with his friend Henk Temming.

Het Goede Doel became one of the most successful Dutch-language groups of the 1980s. The debut album België (1982) sold better that year than any other debut. Hits followed such as In 't leven, Gijzelaar, Eenvoud, Nooduitgang and Vriendschap. Westbroek wrote sharp lyrics, and some broadcasters refused to play songs because they found the subject too sensitive. In 1991 he left after a disagreement with Temming. As a solo artist he started with Voorjaar (1992), and in 1998 he had a big hit with Zelfs je naam is mooi. For others he wrote Toveren for Herman van Veen, among other songs, together with Temming.

Westbroek was more than a singer. For years he presented radio, including Denk aan Henk on 3FM, and at VARA a programme with nothing but hard rock. In Utrecht he had the café Stairway to Heaven, where well-known artists performed. He also went into politics, for Leefbaar Utrecht and Leefbaar Nederland, and left that in 2002. Together with Temming he showed that pop music with Dutch lyrics about ordinary and uncomfortable subjects could reach a large audience.
artiest/henk-westbroek.listen: Listen to Vriendschap by Het Goede Doel. Notice how the lyrics tell a story in plain Dutch, carried by a 1980s pop sound.

artiest/henny-vrienten.text:
Henny Vrienten was born on 27 July 1948 in Hilvarenbeek and grew up in Tilburg, where he had guitar lessons. In the 1960s he played in beat groups such as Les Cruches. In the 1970s he wrote for others and tried his luck as a solo artist, including as Paul Santos, without much success. In Boudewijn de Groot's backing band he met the keyboard player Ernst Jansz, with whom he started the reggae band The Rumbones in 1977.

Jansz then asked him to join his band Doe Maar. Vrienten doubted whether a Dutch-language group could make it, but in 1980 he joined anyway. He became singer and bass player, wrote most of the songs with Jansz and helped design the green and pink sleeve of Skunk (1981), after which those colours became the band's hallmark. In 1982 Doe Maar broke through massively with Doris Day and the group became the face of the new Dutch-language pop wave. In 1984 the band said farewell, and in 1999 a reunion followed.

After Doe Maar, Vrienten chose other work. He wrote music for television and film, including for Sesamstraat and for films such as Abeltje, Kruimeltje and Left Luggage, and he produced other artists. He even collaborated with the rap group Osdorp Posse. With George Kooymans and Boudewijn de Groot he later formed the trio Vreemde Kostgangers. Vrienten died on 25 April 2022.
artiest/henny-vrienten.listen: Listen to Doris Day (1982) by Doe Maar, the song with which the band broke through. Notice the bouncy ska rhythm, with the emphasis on the offbeat, and Vrienten's bass, which makes the song dance.

artiest/henri-belolo.text:
Henri Belolo was a French producer and songwriter from the disco era. He was born in 1936 in Casablanca, into a Jewish-Moroccan family, and as a boy heard the music of American soldiers and of African musicians. In Paris he worked for record boss Eddie Barclay and as a club DJ. At Polydor from 1960 he did artist work and production, with Georges Moustaki and Jeanne Moreau, among others. Later he started his own label Carabine and the music publisher Scorpio Music.

In 1973 Belolo left for New York, where he founded Can't Stop Productions. In early 1975 he met the composer Jacques Morali. Together in Philadelphia they made Brazil by the Ritchie Family, first a club hit and then a worldwide success. Belolo mainly wrote lyrics, Morali the music. In 1977 they came up with Village People, a group that performed with costumed characters playing on stereotypes from New York's gay clubs. Hits such as Y.M.C.A., In the Navy and Go West followed. In 2015 a judge ruled that singer Victor Willis and Morali had written those songs without Belolo, after which his name as a writer had to be removed.

Belolo was not gay himself, but together with Morali he saw the power of the gay club scene as an audience for disco. In doing so he helped launch one of the best-known concepts in disco history. In the 1980s he also produced Break Machine. He remained active as a producer in France until his death in Paris in 2019.
artiest/henri-belolo.listen: Listen to Y.M.C.A. by Village People. Notice the chorus that everyone can sing along to and the solid disco beat beneath it: music made for dancing together.

artiest/henry-grimes.text:
Henry Grimes was an American jazz double bassist and violinist, born on 3 November 1935 in Philadelphia. His parents had both been musicians in their youth. He began on violin at twelve, then played tuba, horn and percussion, among other instruments, and chose the double bass at high school. He studied at Juilliard and by the mid-1950s already had a reputation as a versatile bassist.

Grimes played with Lennie Tristano, Lee Konitz, Gerry Mulligan, Sonny Rollins, Thelonious Monk, McCoy Tyner, Anita O'Day and Benny Goodman. Charles Mingus chose him when he wanted a second bassist in his band. At the 1958 Newport Jazz Festival, captured in the film Jazz on a Summer's Day, he played with six different groups at the age of twenty-two. Later he joined the free jazz movement and worked with Cecil Taylor, Don Cherry, Steve Lacy, Pharoah Sanders, Archie Shepp and Albert Ayler. In 1966 The Call was released on ESP-Disk, his only album as a leader from that period.

Around 1970 he disappeared from the music world and was often presumed dead. In 2002 a social worker and jazz lover found him in Los Angeles, without a bass. He began playing again and recorded new albums, such as Spirits Aloft in 2010. He died on 15 April 2020.
artiest/henry-grimes.listen: Listen to The Call from 1966. Notice how the double bass does not merely accompany, but takes part itself in a conversation with Perry Robinson's clarinet.

artiest/henry-mancini.text: Henry Mancini grew up in Pennsylvania, studied briefly at Juilliard and after the war played in the Glenn Miller Orchestra. At Universal he learned the trade in the studio music department. He contributed to Touch of Evil (1958), among other films. His breakthrough was the TV series Peter Gunn (1958), with a cool jazz score built around a repeated bass line. The album of it won the first Grammy for album of the year. For Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961) he wrote Moon River, which earned Oscars for song and score. Charade (1963) and The Pink Panther (1963) followed, among others. Mancini also turned film music into successful records.
artiest/henry-mancini.listen: Notice the lounge-jazz sound: a steady bass line or a creeping tenor sax, with light strings or a choir over the top.
